Predicting Past-Year Telehealth Use: NHIS 2024 Development and 2025 Temporal Validation

Team 1: CHERY Lab (prediction analysis: Yao Yao)

2026-11-20

# Results were produced with these versions; other versions (especially

print(sapply(c("xgboost", "PRROC", "survey", "grpreg"),
             function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p))))
##   xgboost     PRROC    survey    grpreg 
## "1.7.6.1"   "1.3.1"   "4.2.1"   "3.5.0"

1 Overview

Outcome. VIRAPP12M_A: had a video or phone appointment with a doctor or other health professional in the past 12 months (1 = Yes, 2 = No; 7/8/9 excluded).

Design. The analysis has two phases.

  • Development (2024 only). The 2024 NHIS Sample Adult file is split 80/20 into training and test sets (stratified by outcome), with 5-fold cross-validation inside the training set. Data-based screening (item coverage), variable selection, tuning and model fitting use the training set only. The coding dictionary was drafted from NHIS conventions while viewing predictor distributions in the full 2024 file, but no outcome information. From the 2025 file, only the list of variable names is read, to restrict candidates to items fielded in both years. The 2024 test set is used only to evaluate models whose form was fixed beforehand.
  • Temporal validation (2025). The fixed models are evaluated on the 2025 file, an independent cross-sectional sample of different respondents collected one year later. Variable availability and coding are checked before evaluation; the models are not refit or modified.

Variable selection.

  1. Rule-based screening of every 2024 item: fielded in 2025; at least 90% of 2024 training respondents with a substantive answer; not a survey-administration field; not redundant with a retained item; worded the same way in both years; and not an item whose answer a telehealth visit in the reference period can produce (counseling that may be delivered by video or phone, online contact with a provider).
  2. Outcome-proxy diagnostic. Items that a telehealth visit cannot produce but that may stand in for the outcome (in-person care use, online health activity, treatment, prevention, cost barriers, COVID-19 history) are added one at a time to the theory-based model on the training data. Items contributing more than the strongest theory-based predictor are excluded. Unflagged care-use and access items are kept aside as borderline items for a sensitivity analysis only, because they measure care seeking itself; unflagged COVID-19 history remains an ordinary candidate.
  3. Coding. Screened items are coded with an explicit dictionary (valid codes, nonresponse codes, skip meaning, category grouping, reference level); theory-based items are coded in prepare_nhis(). Codes, labels, universes and question wording were checked against the 2024 and 2025 Sample Adult codebooks (codebook_verification.csv).
  4. Statistical selection among all candidates, with no item forced in: bidirectional stepwise selection by BIC starting from the intercept-only model, with group lasso (every item penalized) as a cross-check and repeated half-sample selection to assess stability. The five covariates of the project dashboard’s association model (age, insurance, education, Internet access, self-rated health) are part of the theory-based set and are treated like every other candidate. Nested cross-validation evaluates the selection and fitting steps given the screened candidate set; screening, coding and the outcome-proxy diagnostic are done once beforehand and are not repeated inside folds.
  5. Two comparisons, with a constant (prevalence-only) model as the lower reference. (a) Full theory-based (Andersen) model vs stepwise BIC within the same 22 items: can the theory-based set be simplified? (b) Theory-based models vs models built from the wider screened pool (stepwise BIC, group lasso, XGBoost): how much do more items and different methods add?

Theory-based set. Andersen’s behavioral model is a conceptual framework without a standard variable list. The 22 items are one operationalization: commonly used predisposing, enabling and need measures available in both NHIS years. It is not a validated standard set. Urban-rural classification, a common enabling factor, was missing from the initial specification by oversight and was added afterwards; because earlier analyses had already shown it to be a strong predictor, this addition was not made blind to the data.

Primary model. The main-effects stepwise BIC model was fixed as the primary model before any test-set or 2025 evaluation. It is a compromise between parsimony and predictive performance, not the best-predicting model: BIC does not directly optimize out-of-sample log loss, stepwise search finds a good model along its search path rather than a guaranteed optimum, and fewer items do not by themselves make a model easier to use in practice. More flexible models (group lasso, including its sparser 1-SE version, and gradient boosting) are reported for comparison. Interaction and borderline-item analyses are exploratory and do not change the primary model.

Weights. Models are fit unweighted as the baseline, and discrimination and accuracy are reported both unweighted (performance in the analysis sample) and survey-weighted (performance for the U.S. adult population represented by the complete-case sample). A sensitivity analysis refits the primary formula with survey weights. Bootstrap intervals resample primary sampling units within strata and apply to the unweighted metrics of the already-fitted models; they reflect the clustered sample but not uncertainty from model training or selection, and they are not a full design-based inference for weighted metrics. The 2025 weighted calibration gap uses a design-based (Taylor linearization) interval from the survey package.

Run time is roughly 1.5 to 2 hours (nested cross-validation and repeated selection dominate). Slow chunks are cached after the first knit, and parallel steps run on macOS and Linux.

2 Data preparation

2.1 Theory-based predictors

The same function prepares both survey years, so the 2025 validation data use the 2024 coding rules.

raw_fields <- c(
  "VIRAPP12M_A", "AGEP_A", "NOTCOV_A", "PRIVATE_A", "EDUCP_A",
  "ACCSSINT_A", "PHSTAT_A", "SEX_A", "HISPALLP_A", "REGION", "MARITAL_A",
  "NATUSBORN_A", "EMPWRKLSW1_A", "POVRATTC_A", "HYPEV_A", "DIBEV_A",
  "ASEV_A", "COPDEV_A", "CANEV_A", "ARTHEV_A", "DEPEV_A", "ANXEV_A",
  "DISAB3_A", "WTFA_A", "PSTRAT", "PPSU"
)

# The five covariates of the project dashboard's association model; part of
# the theory-based set, with no special status in selection.
dashboard_predictors <- c("age", "insurance", "education", "internet", "health")
added_predictors <- c(
  "sex", "race_eth", "region", "marital", "us_born", "worked_last_week",
  "pov_ratio", "hypertension", "diabetes", "asthma", "copd", "cancer",
  "arthritis", "depression", "anxiety", "disability"
)
expanded_predictors <- c(dashboard_predictors, added_predictors)

# Yes (1) / No (2) items; refused, not ascertained, don't know -> NA.
yes_no <- function(x) {
  factor(x, levels = c(2, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
}

# Items with >= 1% "not ascertained" keep an explicit Unknown category.
with_unknown <- function(x, codes, labels) {
  out <- rep("Unknown", length(x))
  for (i in seq_along(codes)) out[x %in% codes[i]] <- labels[i]
  factor(out, levels = c(labels, "Unknown"))
}

prepare_nhis <- function(raw) {
  stopifnot(all(raw_fields %in% names(raw)))
  rows <- which(raw$VIRAPP12M_A %in% c(1, 2))
  d <- raw[rows, ]

  insurance <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(d))
  insured <- d$NOTCOV_A %in% 2
  insurance[d$NOTCOV_A %in% 1] <- "Uninsured"
  insurance[insured & d$PRIVATE_A %in% c(1, 2)] <- "Any private coverage"
  insurance[insured & d$PRIVATE_A %in% 3] <- "Public / other, no private"

  education <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(d))
  education[d$EDUCP_A %in% 0:2] <- "Less than high school"
  education[d$EDUCP_A %in% 3:4] <- "High school / GED"
  education[d$EDUCP_A %in% 5:7] <- "Some college / associate"
  education[d$EDUCP_A %in% 8:10] <- "Bachelor's or higher"

  race_eth <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(d))
  race_eth[d$HISPALLP_A %in% 1] <- "Hispanic"
  race_eth[d$HISPALLP_A %in% 2] <- "NH White"
  race_eth[d$HISPALLP_A %in% 3] <- "NH Black"
  race_eth[d$HISPALLP_A %in% 4] <- "NH Asian"
  race_eth[d$HISPALLP_A %in% 5:7] <- "NH other / multiple"

  data.frame(
    telehealth = as.integer(d$VIRAPP12M_A == 1),
    # AGEP_A 85 = 85 or older (top-coded); 97/98/99 -> NA.
    age = ifelse(d$AGEP_A %in% 18:85, d$AGEP_A, NA_integer_),
    insurance = factor(insurance, levels = c(
      "Any private coverage", "Public / other, no private", "Uninsured"
    )),
    education = factor(education, levels = c(
      "Bachelor's or higher", "Some college / associate",
      "High school / GED", "Less than high school"
    )),
    internet = factor(d$ACCSSINT_A, levels = c(1, 2),
                      labels = c("Internet access", "No internet access")),
    health = factor(d$PHSTAT_A, levels = 1:5,
                    labels = c("Excellent", "Very good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor")),
    sex = factor(d$SEX_A, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    race_eth = factor(race_eth, levels = c(
      "NH White", "Hispanic", "NH Black", "NH Asian", "NH other / multiple"
    )),
    region = factor(d$REGION, levels = 1:4,
                    labels = c("Northeast", "Midwest", "South", "West")),
    marital = with_unknown(d$MARITAL_A, 1:3,
                           c("Married", "Living with partner", "Neither")),
    us_born = with_unknown(d$NATUSBORN_A, 1:2, c("Yes", "No")),
    # Edited recode (accounts for temporary absence and unpaid family work);
    # code 9 (don't know) becomes the Unknown category.
    worked_last_week = with_unknown(d$EMPWRKLSW1_A, 1:2, c("Yes", "No")),
    # 2024 top-codes the ratio at 11; apply the same cap to every year.
    pov_ratio = pmin(d$POVRATTC_A, 11),
    hypertension = yes_no(d$HYPEV_A),
    diabetes = yes_no(d$DIBEV_A),
    asthma = yes_no(d$ASEV_A),
    copd = yes_no(d$COPDEV_A),
    cancer = yes_no(d$CANEV_A),
    arthritis = yes_no(d$ARTHEV_A),
    depression = yes_no(d$DEPEV_A),
    anxiety = yes_no(d$ANXEV_A),
    disability = yes_no(d$DISAB3_A),
    survey_weight = d$WTFA_A,
    survey_stratum = d$PSTRAT,
    survey_psu = d$PPSU,
    source_row = rows
  )
}

2.2 Item labels, screening rules and coding dictionary

Item labels and the coding dictionary were written from NHIS conventions and then checked item by item against the 2024 and 2025 Sample Adult codebooks (codes, labels, universes, question wording; page references in codebook_verification.csv). The dictionary is exported to coding_dictionary.csv. For theory-based items, the dictionary documents the codes used for screening coverage; their analysis coding is done in prepare_nhis().

# ---- Coding dictionary --------------------------------------------------------
# Each entry lists the analysis categories ("groups") and the NHIS codes in
# each, the codes treated as nonresponse (refused, not ascertained, don't
# know), the meaning of a blank (NA) when the item was skipped by design,
# how nonresponse is handled, and the reference category. Nonresponse gets
# its own "Missing" category when it is about 1% or more of 2024
# respondents; otherwise it is assigned to the most common category.
item <- function(groups, missing = c(7, 8, 9), skip = NULL,
                 nonresponse = "Missing", ref = names(groups)[1],
                 type = "categorical", note = "") {
  stopifnot(ref %in% names(groups),
            nonresponse %in% c("Missing", "Exclude", names(groups)))
  list(groups = groups, missing = missing, skip = skip,
       nonresponse = nonresponse, ref = ref, type = type, note = note)
}
yes_no_item <- function(nonresponse = "No", ref = "No", yes = 1, no = 2, ...) {
  item(setNames(list(yes, no), c("Yes", "No")), nonresponse = nonresponse,
       ref = ref, type = "binary", ...)
}
difficulty_item <- function(merge_cannot = FALSE, ...) {
  groups <- if (merge_cannot) {
    list("No difficulty" = 1, "Some difficulty" = 2,
         "A lot of difficulty or cannot do" = 3:4)
  } else {
    list("No difficulty" = 1, "Some difficulty" = 2,
         "A lot of difficulty" = 3, "Cannot do at all" = 4)
  }
  item(groups, nonresponse = "No difficulty", type = "ordinal", ...)
}
frequency_item <- function(...) {
  item(list("Never" = 5, "Daily" = 1, "Weekly" = 2, "Monthly" = 3,
            "A few times a year" = 4), type = "ordinal", ...)
}

coding_dictionary <- list(
  # Theory-based items: the analysis coding is done in
  # prepare_nhis(); these entries document the same rules (categories,
  # reference level, nonresponse handling) and supply the codes used for
  # screening coverage. "Exclude" = nonresponse becomes NA and the
  # respondent leaves the complete-case sample.
  AGEP_A = item(list("Age 18-85" = 18:85), missing = 97:99, type = "continuous",
                nonresponse = "Exclude", note = "85 = 85 or older"),
  NOTCOV_A = item(list("Not covered" = 1, "Covered" = 2), nonresponse = "Exclude",
                  note = "combined with PRIVATE_A into insurance in prepare_nhis()"),
  PRIVATE_A = item(list("Yes" = 1:2, "No" = 3), nonresponse = "Exclude",
                   note = "combined with NOTCOV_A into insurance in prepare_nhis()"),
  EDUCP_A = item(list("Bachelor's or higher" = 8:10, "Less than high school" = 0:2,
                      "High school / GED" = 3:4, "Some college / associate" = 5:7),
                 missing = 97:99, nonresponse = "Exclude"),
  ACCSSINT_A = yes_no_item(ref = "Yes", nonresponse = "Exclude"),
  PHSTAT_A = item(list("Excellent" = 1, "Very good" = 2, "Good" = 3,
                       "Fair" = 4, "Poor" = 5), type = "ordinal",
                  nonresponse = "Exclude"),
  SEX_A = item(list("Male" = 1, "Female" = 2), nonresponse = "Exclude"),
  HISPALLP_A = item(list("NH White" = 2, "Hispanic" = 1, "NH Black" = 3,
                         "NH Asian" = 4, "NH other / multiple" = 5:7),

dictionary_codes <- function(entry) unlist(entry$groups, use.names = FALSE)

# Dictionary in long form, for review against the codebooks.
dictionary_table <- function() {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(coding_dictionary), function(v) {
    e <- coding_dictionary[[v]]
    data.frame(
      variable = v, label = unname(variable_labels[v]), type = e$type,
      category = names(e$groups),
      nhis_codes = vapply(e$groups, function(g) {
        if (length(g) > 4 && all(diff(g) == 1)) sprintf("%g-%g", min(g), max(g))
        else paste(g, collapse = ",")
      }, character(1)),
      reference = names(e$groups) == e$ref,
      nonresponse_codes = paste(e$missing, collapse = ","),
      nonresponse_handling = e$nonresponse,
      skip_meaning = if (is.null(e$skip)) "" else e$skip,
      note = e$note
    )
  }))
}

# Coverage: share of respondents with a substantive answer. Dictionary codes
# are used when available; other items fall back to NHIS reserve-code
# conventions (7/8/9, 97/98/99, ...), which is approximate.
reserve_codes <- function(x) {
  v <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (!length(v)) return(numeric(0))
  d <- nchar(as.character(floor(max(v))))
  top <- 10^d - c(3, 2, 1)
  others <- setdiff(unique(v), top)
  if (length(others) && max(others) >= 10^d - 3) numeric(0) else top
}

item_coverage <- function(v, x) {
  e <- coding_dictionary[[v]]
  if (!is.null(e)) {
    if (e$type == "continuous") {
      g <- e$groups[[1]]
      return(mean(!is.na(x) & x >= min(g) & x <= max(g) & !(x %in% e$missing)))
    }
    return(mean(x %in% dictionary_codes(e)))
  }
  mean(!is.na(x) & !(x %in% reserve_codes(x)))
}

# Screening uses the 2024 data and only the *names* of the 2025 variables
# (which items were fielded in 2025). No 2025 values or outcomes are read.
screen_variables <- function(raw_2024, names_2025, min_coverage = 0.90) {
  outcome_24 <- raw_2024$VIRAPP12M_A %in% c(1, 2)
  vars <- setdiff(names(raw_2024), "VIRAPP12M_A")

  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars, function(v) {
    x <- raw_2024[[v]][outcome_24]
    data.frame(
      variable = v,
      coverage_2024 = if (is.numeric(x)) round(item_coverage(v, x), 3) else NA_real_,
      coverage_basis = if (v %in% names(coding_dictionary)) "dictionary" else
        "reserve-code convention (approximate)",
      share_nonblank_2024 = round(mean(!is.na(x)), 3)
    )
  }))
  out$fielded_2025 <- out$variable %in% names_2025

  low_coverage <- is.na(out$coverage_2024) | out$coverage_2024 < min_coverage
  v <- out$variable

  # Rules are applied in this order and a later rule overrides an earlier
  # one, so the list runs from lowest to highest priority. Theory-based
  # items are kept regardless of coverage (their coverage is reported in the
  # Rmd); final decisions for uncertain items are set after the
  # outcome-proxy diagnostic.
  decision <- rep("Excluded: not reviewed", length(v))
  rules <- list(
    list(v %in% names(coding_dictionary), "Candidate: new"),
    list(v %in% setdiff(uncertain_raw, uncertain_candidate_raw),
         "Uncertain: outcome-proxy check"),
    list(low_coverage, "Excluded: 2024 coverage < 90% (skip pattern)"),
    list(v %in% unverified_raw, "Excluded: label not verified"),
    list(v %in% too_rare_raw, "Excluded: too few respondents in a category"),
    list(v %in% admin_raw, "Excluded: survey administration"),
    list(v %in% redundant_raw, "Excluded: redundant"),
    list(v %in% not_comparable_raw, "Excluded: wording changed in 2025"),
    list(v %in% leakage_raw, "Excluded: answer can come from a telehealth visit"),
    list(v %in% c(core_raw, added16_raw, theory_dictionary_raw),
         "Candidate: theory-based set"),
    list(!out$fielded_2025, "Excluded: not fielded in 2025")
  )
  for (rule in rules) decision[rule[[1]]] <- rule[[2]]
  out$decision <- decision
  out$label <- unname(ifelse(v %in% names(variable_labels), variable_labels[v], ""))
  out[order(out$decision, out$variable),
      c("variable", "label", "decision", "coverage_2024", "coverage_basis",
        "share_nonblank_2024", "fielded_2025")]
}

# ---- Coding --------------------------------------------------------------------
# Apply the dictionary. The rules are fixed in advance and are not learned
# from the data, so the same coding applies inside every CV fold and in 2025.
code_item <- function(x, e, v = "", on_unknown = c("error", "warning")) {
  on_unknown <- match.arg(on_unknown)
  unknown <- !is.na(x) & !(x %in% c(dictionary_codes(e), e$missing))
  if (any(unknown)) {
    msg <- sprintf("%s: %d value(s) with codes not in the dictionary (%s)",
                   v, sum(unknown), paste(sort(unique(x[unknown])), collapse = ","))
    if (on_unknown == "error") stop(msg, call. = FALSE)
    warning(msg, call. = FALSE)
  }
  out <- rep(NA_character_, length(x))
  for (g in names(e$groups)) out[x %in% e$groups[[g]]] <- g
  # A skip label may name an existing category (the skip implies the
  # answer) or a separate "not asked" category.
  skipped <- is.na(x) & !is.null(e$skip)
  if (any(skipped)) out[skipped] <- e$skip
  out[is.na(out)] <- e$nonresponse
  levels <- unique(c(e$ref, setdiff(names(e$groups), e$ref), e$skip,
                     if (e$nonresponse == "Missing") "Missing"))
  factor(out, levels = levels)
}

code_items <- function(raw, vars, on_unknown = "error") {
  as.data.frame(lapply(setNames(vars, vars), function(v) {
    code_item(raw[[v]], coding_dictionary[[v]], v, on_unknown)
  }), stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
}

# Every recode applied to a dataset: several NHIS codes combined into one
# category, nonresponse assigned to a category, and codes not in the
# dictionary (treated as nonresponse).
describe_recodes <- function(raw, vars) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(vars, function(v) {
    e <- coding_dictionary[[v]]
    x <- raw[[v]]
    rows <- list()
    for (g in names(e$groups)) {
      codes <- e$groups[[g]]
      if (length(codes) > 1 && e$type != "continuous") {
        n <- vapply(codes, function(cd) sum(x %in% cd), integer(1))
        rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
          variable = v, action = "combined", codes = paste(codes, collapse = ","),
          n = paste(n, collapse = "/"), coded_as = g)
      }
    }
    unknown <- !is.na(x) & !(x %in% c(dictionary_codes(e), e$missing))
    if (any(unknown)) {
      rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
        variable = v, action = "code not in dictionary",
        codes = paste(sort(unique(x[unknown])), collapse = ","),
        n = as.character(sum(unknown)), coded_as = e$nonresponse)
    }
    coded_nonresp <- x %in% e$missing
    if (any(coded_nonresp)) {
      rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
        variable = v, action = "nonresponse code",
        codes = paste(sort(unique(x[coded_nonresp])), collapse = ","),
        n = as.character(sum(coded_nonresp)), coded_as = e$nonresponse)
    }
    blank_no_rule <- is.na(x) & is.null(e$skip)
    if (any(blank_no_rule)) {
      rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
        variable = v, action = "blank, no skip rule", codes = "blank",
        n = as.character(sum(blank_no_rule)), coded_as = e$nonresponse)
    }
    blank_skip <- is.na(x) & !is.null(e$skip)
    if (any(blank_skip)) {
      rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
        variable = v, action = "blank, skip rule", codes = "blank",
        n = as.character(sum(blank_skip)), coded_as = e$skip)
    }
    do.call(rbind, rows)
  }))
}

2.4 Screening result

Coverage is computed from the predictor values of the 2024 training respondents; the only 2025 information used is the list of variable names (whether an item was fielded in 2025). The screen never uses the outcome or any 2025 values. The full table is written to variable_screening.csv.

# Header row only: the list of items fielded in 2025.
names_2025 <- names(read.csv("adult25.csv", nrows = 0))

screening <- screen_variables(nhis_2024[train_data$source_row, ], names_2025)
write.csv(dictionary_table(), "coding_dictionary.csv", row.names = FALSE)
print(as.data.frame(table(decision = screening$decision)), row.names = FALSE)
##                                           decision Freq
##                                     Candidate: new   67
##                        Candidate: theory-based set   23
##       Excluded: 2024 coverage < 90% (skip pattern)  263
##  Excluded: answer can come from a telehealth visit    3
##                       Excluded: label not verified    4
##                      Excluded: not fielded in 2025  204
##                                Excluded: redundant   30
##                    Excluded: survey administration   13
##        Excluded: too few respondents in a category    1
##                  Excluded: wording changed in 2025    1
##                     Uncertain: outcome-proxy check   20
# Candidate items beyond the theory-based set, and uncertain items that go
# through the outcome-proxy diagnostic below. Every screened item, uncertain
# ones included, is coded so that the diagnostic can use it.
new_candidates <- screening$variable[screening$decision == "Candidate: new"]
uncertain_items <- screening$variable[
  screening$decision == "Uncertain: outcome-proxy check"
]
pool_items <- c(theory_dictionary_raw, new_candidates, uncertain_items)
stopifnot(all(pool_items %in% names(coding_dictionary)))
cat("New candidates:", length(new_candidates),
    "| uncertain items to check:", length(uncertain_items), "\n")
## New candidates: 67 | uncertain items to check: 20
# Theory-based items are kept regardless of coverage; report any below the
# 90% threshold that applies to the other items.
theory_rows <- screening[screening$decision == "Candidate: theory-based set", ]
cat("Theory-based items with 2024 coverage < 90%:",
    if (any(theory_rows$coverage_2024 < 0.9)) {
      paste(theory_rows$variable[theory_rows$coverage_2024 < 0.9], collapse = ", ")
    } else "none", "\n")
## Theory-based items with 2024 coverage < 90%: none
# Items whose coverage is not dictionary-based and whose blanks alone would
# not exclude them: their exclusion rests on the reserve-code convention.
approximate <- screening[screening$coverage_basis != "dictionary" &
                           screening$share_nonblank_2024 >= 0.9 &
                           screening$decision ==
                             "Excluded: 2024 coverage < 90% (skip pattern)", ]
cat("Exclusions resting on approximate coverage:",
    if (nrow(approximate)) paste(approximate$variable, collapse = ", ") else "none",
    "\n")
## Exclusions resting on approximate coverage: WLK13M_A
add_pool <- function(data, raw, on_unknown = "error") {
  cbind(data, code_items(raw[data$source_row, ], pool_items, on_unknown))
}
train_data <- add_pool(train_data, nhis_2024)
test_data <- add_pool(test_data, nhis_2024)

# Smallest category of each item in the training data.
smallest <- sort(vapply(train_data[pool_items], function(f) min(table(f)),
                        integer(1)))
print(head(smallest, 8))
##    OTHGOV_A  UPPSLFCR_A       IHS_A    ORIENT_A    OTHPUB_A SHTFLU12M_A  UPPRAISE_A   COMDIFF_A 
##          53          98         141         143         152         156         164         186

The coding is fixed by the dictionary rather than learned from the data, so it is identical inside every cross-validation fold and in 2025. Several NHIS codes are combined into one category where categories are small or equivalent (for example “cannot do at all” with “a lot of difficulty”; Medicare “yes, no detail” with “yes”). Nonresponse is handled per item as written in the dictionary: a separate “Missing” category when it is about 1% or more of respondents, otherwise assignment to the most common category. Blanks are interpreted as “not asked” only where the dictionary gives a skip rule; other blanks are counted as nonresponse and reported separately below. A code that the dictionary does not list stops the analysis in 2024 and triggers a warning in 2025. Every recode in the training data:

3 Model development (training set only)

3.1 Metrics

log_loss <- function(y, p) {
  p <- pmin(pmax(p, 1e-15), 1 - 1e-15)
  -mean(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log1p(-p))
}

# Mann-Whitney AUROC; tied scores receive average ranks.
auroc <- function(p, y) {
  n1 <- sum(y == 1)
  n0 <- sum(y == 0)
  (sum(rank(p)[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

evaluate_prob <- function(prob, y) {
  auprc <- if (length(unique(prob)) == 1L) {
    mean(y)
  } else {
    pr.curve(scores.class0 = prob[y == 1],
             scores.class1 = prob[y == 0])$auc.integral
  }
  c(log_loss = log_loss(y, prob), AUROC = auroc(prob, y),
    AUPRC = auprc, Brier = mean((y - prob)^2))
}

# Calibration-in-the-large (intercept with slope fixed at 1) and slope.
calibration_stats <- function(prob, y) {
  lp <- qlogis(pmin(pmax(prob, 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6))
  c(
    mean_predicted = mean(prob),
    mean_observed = mean(y),
    cal_intercept = unname(coef(glm(y ~ offset(lp), family = binomial()))[1]),
    cal_slope = unname(coef(glm(y ~ lp, family = binomial()))[2])
  )
}

# Stop on non-convergence, aliased coefficients or non-finite predictions.
# A factor level absent from a fold's training part makes predict() stop
# with a "new levels" error, which is also surfaced rather than ignored.
check_fit <- function(fit, label) {
  if (!fit$converged) stop(label, ": glm did not converge", call. = FALSE)
  if (anyNA(coef(fit))) {
    stop(label, ": aliased coefficients ",
         paste(names(which(is.na(coef(fit)))), collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
  }
  invisible(fit)
}

cv_logistic <- function(formula) {
  vapply(seq_len(k), function(fold) {
    fit <- glm(formula, data = train_data[fold_id != fold, ],
               family = binomial())
    check_fit(fit, paste("fold", fold))
    valid <- train_data[fold_id == fold, ]
    p <- predict(fit, newdata = valid, type = "response")
    stopifnot(all(is.finite(p)))
    log_loss(valid$telehealth, p)
  }, numeric(1))
}

3.2 Candidate model formulas

# The theory-based (Andersen) set: 22 items, including the five covariates
# used in the project dashboard's association model and urban-rural
# classification. None of them has a special status: in every selection
# procedure below they are candidates like any other item.
andersen_terms <- c("ns(age, df = 3)", "insurance", "education", "internet",
                    "health", setdiff(added_predictors, "pov_ratio"),
                    "ns(pov_ratio, df = 3)", theory_dictionary_raw)
f_null <- telehealth ~ 1
f_theory <- reformulate(andersen_terms, response = "telehealth")

3.3 Outcome-proxy diagnostic for uncertain items

Items that a telehealth visit cannot produce, but that may act as proxies for the outcome (in-person care use, online health activity, treatment, prevention, cost barriers, COVID-19 history), are checked on the training data. Each item is added to the theory-based model, and its contribution is compared with that of the strongest theory-based predictor:

  • gain in 5-fold CV log loss when the item is added, against the largest increase in CV log loss when one theory-based item is removed;
  • likelihood-ratio statistic per degree of freedom, against the largest such statistic among theory-based items.

An item that exceeds either benchmark contributes more than any accepted predictor and is excluded as a possible proxy for the outcome. Unflagged EVERCOVD_A remains an ordinary candidate; the other unflagged items describe care use or access and are used only in the borderline sensitivity analysis. The diagnostic uses training outcomes and is not repeated inside the nested cross-validation folds; it can show that an item is suspicious but cannot prove that it is safe.

fit_terms <- function(terms_) {
  glm(reformulate(terms_, response = "telehealth"), data = train_data,
      family = binomial())
}
lr_per_df <- function(terms_full, term) {
  full <- fit_terms(terms_full)
  reduced <- fit_terms(setdiff(terms_full, term))
  (reduced$deviance - full$deviance) / (length(coef(full)) - length(coef(reduced)))
}

theory_cv <- mean(cv_logistic(f_theory))
benchmark <- data.frame(
  term = andersen_terms,
  cv_logloss_change = vapply(andersen_terms, function(t) {
    mean(cv_logistic(reformulate(setdiff(andersen_terms, t), response = "telehealth"))) -
      theory_cv
  }, numeric(1)),
  lr_per_df = vapply(andersen_terms, lr_per_df, numeric(1),
                     terms_full = andersen_terms)
)
gain_threshold <- max(benchmark$cv_logloss_change)
lr_threshold <- max(benchmark$lr_per_df)
cat("Benchmarks: CV log loss", round(gain_threshold, 5),
    "| LR per df", round(lr_threshold, 1), "\n")

  cv_logloss_gain = vapply(check_items, function(v) {
    theory_cv - mean(cv_logistic(reformulate(c(andersen_terms, v),
                                             response = "telehealth")))
  }, numeric(1)),
  lr_per_df = vapply(check_items, function(v) {
    lr_per_df(c(andersen_terms, v), v)
  }, numeric(1))
)
proxy_check$flagged <- proxy_check$cv_logloss_gain > gain_threshold |
  proxy_check$lr_per_df > lr_threshold

3.4 Stepwise selection by BIC (primary)

Bidirectional stepwise search starting from the intercept-only model, with every candidate (theory-based items included) free to enter or leave. The BIC penalty is log(n) per parameter, with each item entering or leaving as a whole (all of its levels together). This main-effects model was fixed as the primary model before any evaluation, as a compromise between parsimony and predictive performance rather than as the best-predicting model. BIC does not directly optimize out-of-sample log loss, and the stepwise search returns a good model along its path, not a guaranteed global optimum.

n_train <- nrow(train_data)
fit_null <- glm(f_null, data = train_data, family = binomial())
fit_bic <- step(fit_null, scope = list(lower = f_null, upper = f_pool),
                direction = "both", k = log(n_train), trace = 0)

bic_terms <- attr(terms(fit_bic), "term.labels")
f_bic <- reformulate(bic_terms, response = "telehealth")

cat("Selected", length(bic_terms), "terms:\n")

                 variable_labels[bic_terms], "(theory-based set)")

3.5 Stepwise BIC within the theory-based items

The same search restricted to the 22 theory-based (Andersen) items. Compared with the full theory-based model, it shows whether that set can be simplified; compared with the primary model, it isolates the contribution of the wider candidate pool.

fit_bic_theory <- step(fit_null, scope = list(lower = f_null, upper = f_theory),
                       direction = "both", k = log(n_train), trace = 0)
bic_theory_terms <- attr(terms(fit_bic_theory), "term.labels")
f_bic_theory <- reformulate(bic_theory_terms, response = "telehealth")

cat("Kept", length(bic_theory_terms), "of", length(andersen_terms),
    "theory-based terms:", paste(bic_theory_terms, collapse = ", "), "\n")

cat("Dropped:", paste(setdiff(andersen_terms, bic_theory_terms), collapse = ", "), "\n")
## Dropped: race_eth, marital, worked_last_week, hypertension, copd

3.6 Group lasso (cross-check)

Each item is one group (all of its dummy columns or spline bases), and every group is penalized. The penalty is tuned with the same 5 folds. Both the lambda.min fit and the sparser 1-SE fit are carried forward to the test-set and 2025 comparisons.

# Build the design from a given set of rows. The terms object carries the
# spline knots of those rows ("predvars"), so any other data get the same
# basis.
build_design <- function(fit_data) {
  terms_object <- terms(model.frame(reformulate(pool_terms), data = fit_data))
  mm <- model.matrix(terms_object, model.frame(terms_object, data = fit_data))
  term_of_column <- attr(terms_object, "term.labels")[attr(mm, "assign")[-1]]
  group_id <- as.integer(factor(term_of_column, levels = unique(term_of_column)))
  list(
    x = mm[, -1, drop = FALSE], term_of_column = term_of_column,
    group_id = group_id,
    matrix_for = function(data) {
      model.matrix(terms_object, model.frame(terms_object, data = data))[, -1, drop = FALSE]
    }
  )
}

train_design <- build_design(train_data)
x_train <- train_design$x
term_of_column <- train_design$term_of_column
group_id <- train_design$group_id
design_matrix <- train_design$matrix_for

set.seed(2026)
cv_glasso <- cv.grpreg(x_train, train_data$telehealth, group = group_id,
                       penalty = "grLasso", family = "binomial",
                       fold = fold_id, nlambda = 60)

i_min <- which.min(cv_glasso$cve)
i_1se <- min(which(cv_glasso$cve <= cv_glasso$cve[i_min] + cv_glasso$cvse[i_min]))

selected_groups <- function(i) {
  b <- cv_glasso$fit$beta[-1, i]
  unique(term_of_column[b != 0])
}
glasso_min_terms <- selected_groups(i_min)
glasso_1se_terms <- selected_groups(i_1se)

print(data.frame(
  rule = c("lambda.min", "lambda.1se"),
  lambda = signif(cv_glasso$lambda[c(i_min, i_1se)], 3),
  cv_logloss = round(cv_glasso$cve[c(i_min, i_1se)] / 2, 5),
  n_terms = c(length(glasso_min_terms), length(glasso_1se_terms))
), row.names = FALSE)
##        rule  lambda cv_logloss n_terms
##  lambda.min 0.00145    0.50504      76
##  lambda.1se 0.00434    0.50736      54
cat("BIC terms not kept by group lasso (1se):",
    setdiff(bic_terms, glasso_1se_terms), "\n")
## BIC terms not kept by group lasso (1se):

3.7 Selection stability

Two separate questions. (1) Is the BIC selection itself stable? Stepwise BIC is rerun on 20 random half-samples of the training set. (2) Which items does a different method favour? Group lasso at the 1-SE penalty is refit on 50 half-samples. The frequencies are descriptive; disagreement between the two methods reflects their different penalties and is not evidence that either is wrong.

run_parallel <- function(x, fun) {
  if (.Platform$OS.type == "unix") {
    check_workers(mclapply(x, fun, mc.cores = n_workers))
  } else {
    lapply(x, fun)
  }
}

n_bic_subsamples <- 20L
set.seed(2026)
bic_subsample_rows <- lapply(seq_len(n_bic_subsamples),
                             function(b) sample.int(n_train, floor(n_train / 2)))

bic_on_rows <- function(rows) {
  half <- train_data[rows, ]
  lower <- f_null
  upper <- f_pool
  # Formulas must look up `half` here, not in the global environment.
  environment(lower) <- environment(upper) <- environment()
  start <- glm(lower, data = half, family = binomial())
  fit <- step(start, scope = list(lower = lower, upper = upper),
              direction = "both", k = log(nrow(half)), trace = 0)
  attr(terms(fit), "term.labels")
}
bic_subsample_terms <- run_parallel(bic_subsample_rows, bic_on_rows)
bic_frequency <- table(factor(unlist(bic_subsample_terms), levels = pool_terms))
cat("Terms selected per half-sample:",
    paste(range(lengths(bic_subsample_terms)), collapse = " to "), "\n")

for (b in seq_len(n_subsamples)) {
  rows <- sample.int(n_train, floor(n_train / 2))
  fit <- grpreg(x_train[rows, ], train_data$telehealth[rows], group = group_id,
                penalty = "grLasso", family = "binomial", lambda = lambda_path)
  beta <- fit$beta[-1, ncol(fit$beta)]
  chosen <- unique(term_of_column[beta != 0])
  glasso_counts[chosen] <- glasso_counts[chosen] + 1
}

3.8 Gradient boosting (XGBoost)

Tuned on the full candidate pool, as a reference for what a flexible method can extract from the screened items. The tuning scores below come from the same folds used to choose depth, learning rate and number of rounds, so they are not unbiased performance estimates.

xgb_matrix <- function(data, vars) {
  x <- model.matrix(reformulate(vars), data = data)
  x[, colnames(x) != "(Intercept)", drop = FALSE]
}

xgb_grid <- expand.grid(max_depth = 1:3, eta = c(0.05, 0.10))
max_rounds <- 8000L

tune_xgb <- function(vars) {
  x <- xgb_matrix(train_data, vars)
  dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(x, label = train_data$telehealth)
  results <- xgb_grid
  results$best_nrounds <- NA_integer_
  results$cv_logloss <- NA_real_

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(results))) {
    params <- list(
      objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "logloss",
      tree_method = "hist", max_depth = results$max_depth[i],
      eta = results$eta[i], min_child_weight = 10
    )
    cv <- xgb.cv(params = params, data = dtrain, folds = validation_folds,
                 nrounds = max_rounds, early_stopping_rounds = 50, verbose = 0)
    loss <- cv$evaluation_log$test_logloss_mean
    results$best_nrounds[i] <- which.min(loss)
    results$cv_logloss[i] <- min(loss)
  }

  stopifnot(all(results$best_nrounds < max_rounds))
  best <- results[which.min(results$cv_logloss), ]
  params <- list(
    objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "logloss",
    tree_method = "hist", max_depth = best$max_depth, eta = best$eta,
    min_child_weight = 10
  )
  list(grid = results[order(results$cv_logloss), ], params = params,
       nrounds = best$best_nrounds, vars = vars)
}

pool_vars <- c(expanded_predictors, theory_dictionary_raw, new_candidates)

set.seed(2026)
xgb_pool <- tune_xgb(pool_vars)
print(xgb_pool$grid, row.names = FALSE)

3.9 Nested cross-validation of the selection procedures

Cross-validating a final selected formula, or a group-lasso fit whose penalty was tuned on the same folds, does not account for the selection step. Here each whole procedure is repeated inside each outer fold, using only the other four folds: stepwise BIC (on the full pool and on the theory-based items) is rerun, and for group lasso the spline basis is rebuilt and the penalty is tuned by an inner 5-fold CV. The held-out fold is used only for scoring. This evaluates the selection and fitting steps given the screened candidate set: screening and dictionary coding are done once beforehand and are not repeated inside folds, and the inner CV of group lasso uses the spline basis of the outer training part. It is therefore not an evaluation of the complete pipeline from the raw file.

run_folds <- function(fun) {
  if (.Platform$OS.type == "unix") {
    check_workers(mclapply(seq_len(k), fun, mc.cores = min(k, n_workers)))
  } else {
    lapply(seq_len(k), fun)
  }
}

nested_bic_fold <- function(fold, upper_formula) {
  inner <- train_data[fold_id != fold, ]
  outer <- train_data[fold_id == fold, ]
  lower <- f_null
  upper <- upper_formula
  # Formulas must look up `inner` here, not in the global environment.
  environment(lower) <- environment(upper) <- environment()
  start <- glm(lower, data = inner, family = binomial())
  fit <- step(start, scope = list(lower = lower, upper = upper),
              direction = "both", k = log(nrow(inner)), trace = 0)
  check_fit(fit, paste("nested BIC, fold", fold))
  p <- predict(fit, newdata = outer, type = "response")
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(p)))
  list(loss = log_loss(outer$telehealth, p),
       terms = attr(terms(fit), "term.labels"))
}

nested_glasso_fold <- function(fold) {
  inner <- train_data[fold_id != fold, ]
  outer <- train_data[fold_id == fold, ]
  design <- build_design(inner)
  set.seed(2026 + fold)
  inner_fold <- integer(nrow(inner))
  for (rows in split(seq_len(nrow(inner)), inner$telehealth)) {
    inner_fold[sample(rows)] <- rep(seq_len(k), length.out = length(rows))
  }
  cv_in <- cv.grpreg(design$x, inner$telehealth, group = design$group_id,
                     penalty = "grLasso", family = "binomial",
                     fold = inner_fold, nlambda = 60)
  j_min <- which.min(cv_in$cve)
  j_1se <- min(which(cv_in$cve <= cv_in$cve[j_min] + cv_in$cvse[j_min]))
  x_out <- design$matrix_for(outer)
  score <- function(j) {
    log_loss(outer$telehealth,
             as.numeric(predict(cv_in$fit, x_out, lambda = cv_in$lambda[j],
                                type = "response")))
  }
  c(lambda_min = score(j_min), lambda_1se = score(j_1se))
}

nested_bic <- run_folds(function(f) nested_bic_fold(f, f_pool))
nested_bic_theory <- run_folds(function(f) nested_bic_fold(f, f_theory))
nested_glasso <- do.call(rbind, run_folds(nested_glasso_fold))

3.10 Comparison of cross-validated performance

For the selection procedures, the nested estimates are the ones to compare. 3.11 Sensitivity: borderline items

Starting from the BIC model, borderline items (uncertain items that passed the outcome-proxy diagnostic but describe care use or access) are offered for forward entry under the same BIC criterion. This analysis is exploratory: the items are selected on the full training set and then cross-validated as a fixed formula, so the reported CV log loss is an apparent value, not comparable with the nested estimates above. It does not change the primary model.

f_bic_border_upper <- reformulate(c(bic_terms, borderline_candidates),
                                  response = "telehealth")
fit_border <- step(fit_bic, scope = list(lower = f_bic, upper = f_bic_border_upper),
                   direction = "forward", k = log(n_train), trace = 0)
border_added <- setdiff(attr(terms(fit_border), "term.labels"),
                        bic_terms)
cat("Borderline items entering:",
    if (length(border_added)) paste(border_added, collapse = ", ") else "none", "\n")

    apparent_cv_logloss_bic = mean(cv_logistic(f_bic)),

Survey-weighted versions of the same metrics describe performance for the population represented by the complete-case test respondents (weights are the original NHIS adult weights; complete-case exclusion is not reweighted).

# Weighted Mann-Whitney AUROC: sum over positive-negative pairs of
# w_i * w_j * [p_i > p_j] (ties count one half), divided by the product of
# the positive and negative weight totals.
weighted_auroc <- function(p, y, w) {
  g <- match(p, sort(unique(p)))
  w_pos <- tapply(w * (y == 1), g, sum)
  w_neg <- tapply(w * (y == 0), g, sum)
  below <- cumsum(w_neg) - w_neg
  sum(w_pos * (below + 0.5 * w_neg)) / (sum(w_pos) * sum(w_neg))
}

weighted_metrics <- function(prob, y, w) {
  p <- pmin(pmax(prob, 1e-15), 1 - 1e-15)
  w <- w / sum(w)
  c(log_loss = -sum(w * (y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log1p(-p))),
    AUROC = weighted_auroc(prob, y, w),
    Brier = sum(w * (y - prob)^2))
}

stopifnot(abs(weighted_auroc(test_prob[[primary_model]], y_test,
                             rep(1, length(y_test))) -
                auroc(test_prob[[primary_model]], y_test)) < 1e-10)

4.1 Bootstrap confidence intervals

Paired bootstrap with 1,000 replicates. Within each NHIS stratum, primary sampling units (PSUs) are drawn with replacement and all of their sampled respondents are kept, so the intervals account for stratified cluster sampling. They apply to the unweighted metrics of models that are already fitted: they do not include uncertainty from training or variable selection, and they are not a full design-based inference for weighted metrics (which would use replicate weights or linearization). Gains are positive when the primary model is better.

# Row indices grouped by PSU within stratum.
psu_index <- function(data) {
  key <- paste(data$survey_stratum, data$survey_psu)
  rows_by_psu <- split(seq_len(nrow(data)), key)
  stratum_of_psu <- sub(" .*", "", names(rows_by_psu))
  split(rows_by_psu, stratum_of_psu)
}

draw_psu_sample <- function(index) {
  unlist(lapply(index, function(psus) {
    psus[sample.int(length(psus), length(psus), replace = TRUE)]
  }), use.names = FALSE)
}

bootstrap_compare <- function(prob, y, index, B = 1000, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  primary <- prob[[primary_model]]
  comparators <- c("Theory-based logistic",
                   "Theory-based BIC logistic", "Group lasso (lambda.min)",
                   "Group lasso (lambda.1se)", "Full pool XGBoost")
  draws <- replicate(B, {
    i <- draw_psu_sample(index)
    a_primary <- auroc(primary[i], y[i])
    l_primary <- log_loss(y[i], primary[i])
    c(primary_AUROC = a_primary,
      unlist(lapply(setNames(comparators, comparators), function(m) {
        c(AUROC_gain = a_primary - auroc(prob[[m]][i], y[i]),
          logloss_gain = log_loss(y[i], prob[[m]][i]) - l_primary)
      })))
  })
  t(apply(draws, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)))
}

test_psu_index <- psu_index(test_data)
cat("Test set:", length(test_psu_index), "strata,",
    sum(lengths(test_psu_index)), "PSUs\n")
## Test set: 52 strata, 659 PSUs
print(round(bootstrap_compare(test_prob, y_test, test_psu_index), 4))

## Stepwise BIC logistic             0.2540        0.2565        0.0151    0.9288

calibration_by_band <- function(prob, y, weight = rep(1, length(y))) {
  band <- cut(prob, breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.10), include.lowest = TRUE)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(split(seq_along(prob), band, drop = TRUE),
                        function(rows) {
    w <- weight[rows]
    data.frame(
      n = length(rows),
      weighted_share_pct = 100 * sum(w) / sum(weight),
      predicted = weighted.mean(prob[rows], w),
      observed = weighted.mean(y[rows], w),
      gap_pp = 100 * (weighted.mean(y[rows], w) - weighted.mean(prob[rows], w))
    )
  }))
}

cal_test <- calibration_by_band(test_prob[[primary_model]], y_test)
print(round(cal_test, 4))

raw_items_of <- function(vars) {
  items <- ifelse(vars %in% names(raw_item_map), raw_item_map[vars], vars)
  unique(c(items, if ("insurance" %in% vars) "PRIVATE_A"))
}

  "Stepwise BIC logistic" = raw_items_of(all.vars(f_bic)[-1]),

  "Borderline items (sensitivity)" = borderline_candidates
)

  items = lengths(model_items),
  missing_in_2025 = vapply(model_items, function(x) {

  }, character(1))
)

Response codes in 2025 are compared with the coding dictionary. A code that the dictionary does not list triggers a warning and is treated as nonresponse: for screened items it receives the item’s nonresponse handling; for theory-based items it becomes missing and the respondent drops out of the complete-case sample. Codes listed in the dictionary but absent in 2025 are also reported.

check_coding <- function(item) {
  e <- coding_dictionary[[item]]
  x25 <- nhis_2025[[item]][valid_2025]
  observed <- x25[!is.na(x25) & !(x25 %in% e$missing)]
  if (e$type == "continuous") {
    g <- e$groups[[1]]
    outside <- observed[observed < min(g) | observed > max(g)]
    return(data.frame(
      item = item, coverage_2025 = round(item_coverage(item, x25), 3),
      not_in_dictionary = if (length(outside)) sprintf("%g to %g", min(outside),
                                                       max(outside)) else "",
      n_not_in_dictionary = length(outside), absent_in_2025 = ""))
  }
  codes <- dictionary_codes(e)
  unknown <- sort(unique(observed[!(observed %in% codes)]))
  data.frame(
    item = item, coverage_2025 = round(item_coverage(item, x25), 3),
    not_in_dictionary = paste(unknown, collapse = ","),
    n_not_in_dictionary = sum(observed %in% unknown),
    absent_in_2025 = paste(setdiff(codes, observed), collapse = ",")
  )
}

coding_check <- do.call(rbind, lapply(model_items[["Group lasso / full pool XGBoost"]],
                                      check_coding))
coding_check$in_primary_model <- coding_check$item %in%
  model_items[["Stepwise BIC logistic"]]
coding_check$label <- unname(ifelse(coding_check$item %in% names(variable_labels),

Design-based 95% CI for the weighted calibration gap (observed minus predicted, percentage points). The full survey design is built first and the validation sample is then treated as a domain.

design_rows <- validation_2025$source_row
stopifnot(all(nhis_2025$WTFA_A[design_rows] == weight_2025))

nhis_2025$in_validation <- FALSE
nhis_2025$in_validation[design_rows] <- TRUE

weighted_gap <- function(model_name) {
  nhis_2025$gap_pp <- NA_real_
  nhis_2025$gap_pp[design_rows] <- 100 * (y_2025 - prob_2025[[model_name]])
  design <- svydesign(ids = ~PPSU, strata = ~PSTRAT, weights = ~WTFA_A,
                      data = nhis_2025, nest = TRUE)
  domain <- subset(design, in_validation)
  est <- svymean(~gap_pp, domain)
  ci <- confint(est, df = degf(domain))
  c(gap_pp = unname(coef(est)), lower_95 = ci[1, 1], upper_95 = ci[1, 2])
}

gap_table <- t(vapply(
  c("Theory-based logistic", "Theory-based BIC logistic", primary_model),
  weighted_gap, numeric(3)
))
print(round(gap_table, 3))

6 Sensitivity: survey-weighted model fitting

The primary formula is refit with the NHIS adult weights (rescaled to mean 1; quasibinomial family, so point estimates equal weighted maximum likelihood). Variable selection is not repeated. Both versions are scored unweighted and weighted in the 2024 test set and in 2025.

train_w <- train_data$survey_weight / mean(train_data$survey_weight)
fit_primary_weighted <- glm(f_bic, data = train_data, family = quasibinomial(),
                            weights = train_w)

score_versions <- function(data, y, w) {
  p_unw <- unname(predict(fit_primary, data, type = "response"))
  p_w <- unname(predict(fit_primary_weighted, data, type = "response"))
  rbind(
    "Unweighted fit, unweighted metrics" = evaluate_prob(p_unw, y)[c("log_loss", "AUROC", "Brier")],
    "Weighted fit, unweighted metrics" = evaluate_prob(p_w, y)[c("log_loss", "AUROC", "Brier")],
    "Unweighted fit, weighted metrics" = weighted_metrics(p_unw, y, w),
    "Weighted fit, weighted metrics" = weighted_metrics(p_w, y, w)
  )
}

7 Sensitivity: collinearity and interactions

7.1 Collinearity

Generalized variance inflation factors (Fox and Monette), computed from the correlation of the coefficient estimates as in car::vif(). For an item with df parameters, GVIF^(1/(2·df)) is comparable to the square root of a classic VIF; values above about 2.2 (VIF > 5) deserve attention.

gvif_table <- function(fit) {
  R <- cov2cor(vcov(fit)[-1, -1])
  assign <- attr(model.matrix(fit), "assign")[-1]
  labels <- attr(terms(fit), "term.labels")
  det_R <- det(R)
  out <- t(vapply(seq_along(labels), function(j) {
    idx <- which(assign == j)
    g <- det(R[idx, idx, drop = FALSE]) * det(R[-idx, -idx, drop = FALSE]) / det_R
    c(df = length(idx), GVIF = g, GVIF_adjusted = g^(1 / (2 * length(idx))))
  }, numeric(3)))
  out <- data.frame(term = labels, round(out, 3))
  out[order(-out$GVIF_adjusted), ]
}

Several items with large raw GVIFs have a Missing/Unknown category. One possible explanation is that largely the same respondents (about 3%) are unascertained on several of these items; the cross-tabulation below checks how much these categories overlap. This is a diagnostic, not a proof of the source of the inflation.

# Respondents in the Missing/Unknown category of at least one item, and of
# every item, in each group of items with high GVIF.
missing_overlap <- function(data, items, level) {
  flags <- vapply(items, function(v) data[[v]] == level, logical(nrow(data)))
  c(any_item = sum(rowSums(flags) > 0), all_items = sum(rowSums(flags) == length(items)))
}
print(rbind(
  "Primary: voted / public meeting (Missing)" =
    missing_overlap(train_data, c("CEVOTELC_A", "CEMMETNG_A"), "Missing"),
  "Theory-based: marital / U.S.-born / worked (Unknown)" =
    missing_overlap(train_data, c("marital", "us_born", "worked_last_week"), "Unknown")
))

Pairwise association between the predictors of the primary model (Cramér’s V; continuous variables split into quartiles):

as_categories <- function(x) {
  if (is.numeric(x)) cut(x, unique(quantile(x, 0:4 / 4)), include.lowest = TRUE) else x
}
cramers_v <- function(a, b) {
  tab <- table(as_categories(a), as_categories(b))
  chi2 <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE)$statistic)
  unname(sqrt(chi2 / (sum(tab) * (min(dim(tab)) - 1))))
}

primary_vars <- all.vars(f_bic)[-1]
var_pairs <- t(combn(primary_vars, 2))
association <- data.frame(
  var1 = var_pairs[, 1], var2 = var_pairs[, 2],
  cramers_v = round(apply(var_pairs, 1, function(p) {
    cramers_v(train_data[[p[1]]], train_data[[p[2]]])
  }), 3)
)
print(head(association[order(-association$cramers_v), ], 12), row.names = FALSE)

7.2 Pairwise interactions

This analysis is exploratory. All pairwise interactions among the terms of each model are screened in one pass (change in BIC when each is added alone); those that lower BIC are then offered to a forward stepwise BIC search. Selection uses the full training set, and the resulting formula is then cross-validated, so the CV log loss is an apparent value that is not comparable with the nested estimates.

select_interactions <- function(fit) {
  labels <- attr(terms(fit), "term.labels")
  candidates <- apply(t(combn(labels, 2)), 1, paste, collapse = ":")
  screen <- add1(fit, scope = reformulate(c(labels, candidates)),
                 k = log(n_train))[-1, ]
  base_bic <- extractAIC(fit, k = log(n_train))[2]
  screen <- data.frame(interaction = rownames(screen), df = screen$Df,
                       delta_BIC = screen$AIC - base_bic)
  screen <- screen[order(screen$delta_BIC), ]

  passed <- screen$interaction[screen$delta_BIC < 0]
  final_formula <- formula(fit)
  if (length(passed)) {
    upper <- update(formula(fit), paste(". ~ . +", paste(passed, collapse = " + ")))
    final_fit <- step(fit, scope = list(lower = formula(fit), upper = upper),
                      direction = "forward", k = log(n_train), trace = 0)
    final_formula <- formula(final_fit)
  }
  added <- setdiff(attr(terms(final_formula), "term.labels"), labels)
  list(screen = screen, n_candidates = length(candidates),
       added = added, formula = final_formula)
}

interactions <- list(
  "Stepwise BIC" = select_interactions(fit_primary),
  "Theory-based" = select_interactions(fit_theory)
)

for (m in names(interactions)) {
  x <- interactions[[m]]
  cat("\n", m, "model:", sum(x$screen$delta_BIC < 0), "of", x$n_candidates,
      "interactions lower BIC when added alone\n")
  shown <- head(x$screen, 10)
  shown$delta_BIC <- round(shown$delta_BIC, 1)
  print(shown, row.names = FALSE)
  cat("Entered by forward BIC:",
      if (length(x$added)) paste(x$added, collapse = ", ") else "none", "\n")
}

  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("Main effects", "With interactions"), function(version) {
    f <- if (version == "Main effects") base_formulas[[m]] else interactions[[m]]$formula

      apparent_cv_logloss = round(mean(cv_logistic(f)), 5),
      test_logloss = round(log_loss(y_test, p_test), 4),
      test_AUROC = round(auroc(p_test, y_test), 4),
      logloss_2025 = round(log_loss(y_2025, p_2025), 4),
      AUROC_2025 = round(auroc(p_2025, y_2025), 4)
    )
  }))
}))

The primary model remains the main-effects model fixed before evaluation; the interaction results do not change it and are not used to choose between model structures.

8 Interpretation of the primary model

Odds ratios from the stepwise BIC model (unweighted, training set). They describe adjusted associations useful for prediction, are conditional on the selected model (post-selection intervals are too narrow), and are not causal effects or population estimates. The intervals ignore the survey design and the selection step, so they should not be used to call any predictor a significant risk factor. Category names come from the coding dictionary.

coefs <- summary(fit_primary)$coefficients
keep <- !grepl("^\\(Intercept\\)|^ns\\(", rownames(coefs))
or_table <- data.frame(
  term = rownames(coefs)[keep],
  OR = exp(coefs[keep, "Estimate"]),
  lower_95 = exp(coefs[keep, "Estimate"] - 1.96 * coefs[keep, "Std. Error"]),
  upper_95 = exp(coefs[keep, "Estimate"] + 1.96 * coefs[keep, "Std. Error"])
)
or_table$item <- vapply(or_table$term, function(t) {
  hit <- names(variable_labels)[startsWith(t, names(variable_labels))]
  if (length(hit)) variable_labels[hit[which.max(nchar(hit))]] else ""
}, character(1))
print(or_table, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)

The curves below are reference-profile predictions: predicted probability for one hypothetical adult whose other predictors are fixed at the most common category (or the median). They show the shape of the spline terms; they are not population-average effects.

model_vars <- all.vars(f_bic)[-1]
reference_profile <- train_data[1, model_vars]
for (v in model_vars) {
  x <- train_data[[v]]
  reference_profile[[v]] <- if (is.factor(x)) {
    factor(names(which.max(table(x))), levels = levels(x))
  } else median(x)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
if ("age" %in% model_vars) {
  age_grid <- reference_profile[rep(1, 68), ]
  age_grid$age <- 18:85
  plot(18:85, predict(fit_primary, age_grid, type = "response"), type = "l",
       lwd = 2, col = "#B31B1B", xlab = "Age (years)",
       ylab = "Predicted probability (reference profile)", main = "Age")
}
if ("pov_ratio" %in% model_vars) {
  pov_seq <- seq(0, 11, by = 0.1)
  pov_grid <- reference_profile[rep(1, length(pov_seq)), ]
  pov_grid$pov_ratio <- pov_seq
  plot(pov_seq, predict(fit_primary, pov_grid, type = "response"), type = "l",
       lwd = 2, col = "#B31B1B", xlab = "Family income / poverty threshold",
       ylab = "Predicted probability (reference profile)",
       main = "Income-to-poverty ratio")
}

)

9 Model export

The fitted models are written to model_export/ so that they can be reported in full (TRIPOD) and applied to new data without rerunning this document. The logistic and group lasso models are exported as coefficient tables, together with the spline knots and factor levels estimated from the 2024 training data; the XGBoost model is saved in xgboost’s JSON format. Full R model objects are not saved, because they contain a copy of the training data. The standalone scoring function below reads only the exported files; the last chunk checks that it reproduces the 2025 predictions of every exported model.

export_dir <- "model_export"
dir.create(export_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Coefficients. Column names follow R's model.matrix() naming: a factor
# level is the variable name followed by the level label, and a spline
# basis is the term followed by 1, 2, 3. The first level of each factor is
# the reference category.
logistic_fits <- list(
  "Theory-based logistic" = fit_theory,
  "Theory-based BIC logistic" = fit_theory_bic,
  "Stepwise BIC logistic" = fit_primary
)
logistic_coefficients <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(logistic_fits), function(m) {
  fit <- logistic_fits[[m]]
  stopifnot(!anyNA(coef(fit)))
  assign_ <- attr(model.matrix(fit), "assign")
  data.frame(
    model = m,
    term = c("(Intercept)", attr(terms(fit), "term.labels"))[assign_ + 1],
    column = names(coef(fit)),
    estimate = unname(coef(fit)),
    std_error = unname(sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))))
  )
}))

# Group lasso: penalized estimates on the original scale, nonzero groups
# only. No standard errors are defined for these estimates.
glasso_coefficients <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  list("Group lasso (lambda.min)" = i_min, "Group lasso (lambda.1se)" = i_1se),
  function(i) {
    b <- coef(cv_glasso$fit, lambda = cv_glasso$lambda[i])
    stopifnot(identical(names(b)[-1], colnames(x_train)))
    keep <- c(TRUE, b[-1] != 0)
    data.frame(
      term = c("(Intercept)", term_of_column)[keep],
      column = names(b)[keep],
      estimate = unname(b[keep]),
      std_error = NA_real_
    )
  }))
glasso_coefficients$model <- sub("\\.[0-9]+$", "", rownames(glasso_coefficients))
glasso_coefficients <- glasso_coefficients[, names(logistic_coefficients)]

model_coefficients <- rbind(logistic_coefficients, glasso_coefficients)
rownames(model_coefficients) <- NULL
write.csv(model_coefficients, file.path(export_dir, "model_coefficients.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)

# Spline knots (quantiles of the 2024 training data). All models were fit to
# the same rows, so they share one set of knots.
spline_knots <- function(fit) {
  calls <- as.list(attr(terms(fit), "predvars"))[-1]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(calls, function(e) {
    if (!is.call(e) || !deparse(e[[1]]) %in% c("ns", "splines::ns")) return(NULL)
    v <- deparse(e[[2]])
    rbind(data.frame(variable = v, type = "interior", value = unname(eval(e$knots))),
          data.frame(variable = v, type = "boundary",
                     value = unname(eval(e$Boundary.knots))))
  }))
}
knots_table <- spline_knots(fit_theory)
sort_knots <- function(k) k[order(k$variable, k$type, k$value), "value"]
for (fit in logistic_fits) {
  k <- spline_knots(fit)
  stopifnot(identical(sort_knots(k),
                      sort_knots(knots_table[knots_table$variable %in% k$variable, ])))
}
write.csv(knots_table, file.path(export_dir, "spline_knots.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(knots_table, row.names = FALSE)

##        age interior 43.000000

# Factor levels, in model order (the first level is the reference).
model_vars_all <- unique(sub("^ns\\(([^,]+),.*$", "\\1",
                             setdiff(model_coefficients$term, "(Intercept)")))
factor_vars <- model_vars_all[vapply(model_vars_all,
                                     function(v) is.factor(train_data[[v]]),
                                     logical(1))]
for (m in names(logistic_fits)) {
  xl <- logistic_fits[[m]]$xlevels
  for (v in names(xl)) stopifnot(identical(xl[[v]], levels(train_data[[v]])))
}
factor_levels <- do.call(rbind, lapply(factor_vars, function(v) {
  lev <- levels(train_data[[v]])
  data.frame(variable = v, level_order = seq_along(lev), level = lev,
             reference = seq_along(lev) == 1)
}))
write.csv(factor_levels, file.path(export_dir, "factor_levels.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# XGBoost: model file, input columns and tuning result.
invisible(xgb.save(xgb_pool_fit, file.path(export_dir, "xgb_full_pool.json")))
write.csv(data.frame(feature = colnames(xgb_matrix(train_data, pool_vars))),
          file.path(export_dir, "xgb_features.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(setting = c(names(xgb_pool$params), "nrounds"),
                     value = c(vapply(xgb_pool$params, as.character, ""),
                               as.character(xgb_pool$nrounds))),
          file.path(export_dir, "xgb_settings.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Coding rules needed to prepare the raw NHIS items.
invisible(file.copy("coding_dictionary.csv", export_dir, overwrite = TRUE))

The scoring function is written to model_export/predict_from_csv.R. It expects data in which the model variables are already coded as in this analysis (coding dictionary; age in years; income-to-poverty ratio capped at 11).

# Predicted probability of past-year telehealth use from the exported
# coefficient tables (HINF 5001, Team 1 prediction models).
#
# data:  one row per respondent. Every variable the model uses must already
#        be coded as in the analysis (see coding_dictionary.csv): age in
#        years; pov_ratio capped at 11; categorical variables as character
#        or factor using the labels in factor_levels.csv.
# model: a model name in model_coefficients.csv, for example
#        "Stepwise BIC logistic".
predict_from_csv <- function(data, model, export_dir = "model_export") {
  read <- function(f) read.csv(file.path(export_dir, f), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  coefs <- read("model_coefficients.csv")
  coefs <- coefs[coefs$model == model, ]
  if (nrow(coefs) == 0) stop("Unknown model: ", model)
  factor_levels <- read("factor_levels.csv")
  factor_levels <- factor_levels[order(factor_levels$variable,
                                       factor_levels$level_order), ]
  knots <- read("spline_knots.csv")

  columns <- list()
  for (term in setdiff(unique(coefs$term), "(Intercept)")) {
    if (startsWith(term, "ns(")) {
      v <- sub("^ns\\(([^,]+),.*$", "\\1", term)
      k <- knots[knots$variable == v, ]
      basis <- splines::ns(data[[v]],
                           knots = k$value[k$type == "interior"],
                           Boundary.knots = k$value[k$type == "boundary"])
      for (j in seq_len(ncol(basis))) columns[[paste0(term, j)]] <- basis[, j]
    } else if (term %in% factor_levels$variable) {
      lev <- factor_levels$level[factor_levels$variable == term]
      x <- as.character(data[[term]])
      unknown <- setdiff(unique(x[!is.na(x)]), lev)
      if (length(unknown)) {
        stop("Unknown level(s) of ", term, ": ", paste(unknown, collapse = ", "))
      }
      for (l in lev[-1]) columns[[paste0(term, l)]] <- as.numeric(x == l)
    } else {
      columns[[term]] <- as.numeric(data[[term]])
    }
  }
  x <- do.call(cbind, columns)

  beta <- setNames(coefs$estimate, coefs$column)
  slope <- beta[names(beta) != "(Intercept)"]
  absent <- setdiff(names(slope), colnames(x))
  if (length(absent)) stop("Columns not built: ", paste(absent, collapse = ", "))
  eta <- beta[["(Intercept)"]] + drop(x[, names(slope), drop = FALSE] %*% slope)
  plogis(eta)
}

A short README is written alongside the files.

# Exported prediction models: past-year telehealth use (NHIS)

Models developed on the NHIS 2024 adult file (80% training split, seed 2026)
and temporally validated on the NHIS 2025 adult file. Generated by
`nhis_telehealth_prediction_final.Rmd`; see that document for methods.

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `model_coefficients.csv` | Intercept and coefficients (log-odds scale) of the theory-based, theory-based BIC and primary (stepwise BIC) logistic models, with standard errors; nonzero penalized coefficients of the two group lasso models (no standard errors) |
| `spline_knots.csv` | Interior and boundary knots of the natural splines `ns(age, df = 3)` and `ns(pov_ratio, df = 3)` (2024 training data) |
| `factor_levels.csv` | Levels of each categorical variable; the first level is the reference |
| `coding_dictionary.csv` | Rules that turn raw NHIS codes into the model variables, including nonresponse and skip handling |
| `predict_from_csv.R` | `predict_from_csv(data, model)`: predicted probabilities from the files above |
| `xgb_full_pool.json`, `xgb_features.csv`, `xgb_settings.csv` | XGBoost model (xgboost JSON format), its input columns (R `model.matrix` dummy coding) and tuning settings |

Input data must be coded as in the analysis: age in years, income-to-poverty
ratio capped at 11, categorical variables labelled as in `factor_levels.csv`.
Models were fit without survey weights. Predictions describe the NHIS adult
population of 2024–2025 and have not been validated outside this survey.
Raw NHIS files are not included; they are available from the National
Center for Health Statistics.
# Reproduce the 2025 predictions from the exported files alone.
scorer <- new.env()
sys.source(file.path(export_dir, "predict_from_csv.R"), envir = scorer)
export_check <- data.frame(model = unique(model_coefficients$model))
export_check$max_abs_difference <- vapply(export_check$model, function(m) {
  max(abs(scorer$predict_from_csv(validation_2025, m, export_dir) - prob_2025[[m]]))
}, numeric(1))

xgb_reloaded <- xgb.load(file.path(export_dir, "xgb_full_pool.json"))
export_check <- rbind(export_check, data.frame(
  model = "Full pool XGBoost",
  max_abs_difference = max(abs(
    predict(xgb_reloaded, xgb.DMatrix(xgb_matrix(validation_2025, pool_vars))) -
      prob_2025[["Full pool XGBoost"]]))
))
print(export_check, row.names = FALSE)

##      Theory-based logistic       6.661338e-16
##  Theory-based BIC logistic       1.443290e-15
##      Stepwise BIC logistic       1.887379e-15
##   Group lasso (lambda.min)       1.110223e-15
##   Group lasso (lambda.1se)       1.276756e-15
##          Full pool XGBoost       0.000000e+00
stopifnot(export_check$max_abs_difference < 1e-6)
list.files(export_dir)

## [5] "predict_from_csv.R"     "spline_knots.csv"       "xgb_features.csv"       "xgb_full_pool.json"    
## [9] "xgb_settings.csv"

10 Limitations

  • Prior viewing of evaluation data. In the current pipeline, development uses only 2024 training data and the list of 2025 variable names. Earlier iterations of this project, however, examined results in both the 2024 test set and the 2025 file (including before the decision to expand the predictor set), and the coding dictionary was drafted while viewing predictor distributions in the full 2024 file. Neither evaluation set should therefore be described as untouched or fully independent; the 2025 analysis is a temporal validation by the development team.
  • Scope of the validation. The 2025 file tests transportability to the next year of the same survey and questionnaire, not to other populations or data sources.
  • What nested CV covers. Nested CV repeats variable selection and model fitting inside folds, but not screening, coding or the outcome-proxy diagnostic (which uses training outcomes), and the inner CV of group lasso shares the spline basis of the outer training part. XGBoost tuning was not nested; its tuning scores are reported separately. Interaction and borderline-item analyses select on the full training set and report apparent CV values.
  • Uncertainty intervals. Bootstrap intervals resample PSUs within strata for unweighted metrics of fixed models; they exclude uncertainty from training and selection and are not design-based intervals for weighted metrics.
  • Weights and missing data. Models are fit unweighted; weighted metrics and a weighted refit are reported. Weighted results represent the complete-case population; the original weights do not correct for exclusion of respondents with missing predictors.
  • Coding and item classification. The coding dictionary was checked against the 2024 and 2025 codebooks; the check should still be spot-checked by the team. Nonresponse is assigned to the most common category for items with little nonresponse, which can misclassify a small number of respondents. Excluding items whose answer a telehealth visit can produce is a judgment about question content; the outcome-proxy diagnostic can flag suspicious items but cannot prove that an unflagged item is free of leakage. Care-use and access items that passed the diagnostic are examined only in a sensitivity analysis.
  • Theory-based specification. The 22 theory-based items are one operationalization of Andersen’s model, not a standard variable set, and cover individual predisposing, enabling and need factors plus urban-rural classification, but not other contextual factors or health behaviors. Urban-rural classification was added after earlier analyses had shown it to be a strong predictor, so the theory-based set is not fully specified independently of the data.
  • Income and year-specific coding. The income-to-poverty ratio is based on the first of 10 income imputations and is top-coded at 11 in 2024 and 12 in 2025; it is capped at 11 for both years.
  • Selection stability. Some selected items are not reselected in every fold or half-sample (see the stability tables); the primary model should be read as one good parsimonious model, not the unique correct one.
  • Post-selection inference. Odds ratios and their intervals are conditional on the selected model, ignore the survey design, and describe associations, not causal effects.
  • Software environment. Package versions are printed but not locked; other versions (notably of xgboost) may give slightly different results.

11 Summary

  • Item pool: 629 items in the 2024 file, 425 of them also fielded in 2025; 89 candidate terms after screening (including the 22 theory-based terms); excluded by the outcome-proxy diagnostic: HITTEST_A, RX12M_A, HITLOOK_A, LASTDR_A.
  • Primary model (stepwise BIC from the intercept-only model): 23 terms. Stepwise BIC within the theory-based items kept 17 of 22 terms.
  • CV log loss (nested for selection procedures; XGBoost tuning score not ranked): theory-based all items 0.5142, theory-based BIC 0.5145, primary 0.5092, group lasso 0.5051.
  • AUROC, 2024 test: theory-based 0.697, theory-based BIC 0.698, primary 0.713.
  • AUROC, 2025: theory-based 0.704, theory-based BIC 0.704, primary 0.717.
  • 2025 survey-weighted calibration gap (observed − predicted) for the primary model: 0.65 percentage points (95% CI -0.15 to 1.44).
  • Exploratory interactions entering the primary model by forward BIC: anxiety:ns(age, df = 3), depression:arthritis, MILITARY_A:sex, depression:sex; 2025 AUROC 0.7173 without vs 0.7187 with interactions.
